text: "He made Him… to be sin… that we might become the righteousness of God." Two different Greek words for made.
explanation:
The first "made," poieo, means to fashion, the way an artist crafts something; it's the root of poiema, "workmanship," from which we get poem. There was divine artistry in the way God laid all our sins on His Son. The second word, ginomai, means to come into being, something that never existed before, like a birth.

When you were born again, you were born righteous: a new creation "created in righteousness and true holiness," a living poem declaring His excellencies. You didn't make yourself; "we are His workmanship." So stop trying to improve yourself by your own efforts. Look to the One who creates beautifully.

text: Leviticus calls the burnt offering "holy," but the sin offering "most holy." Even bearing our sin, Jesus was most holy.
explanation:
The burnt offering pictures Christ offering Himself wholly to glorify the Father. But in the sin offering we see Him made sin for us, and our thoughts might drift into seeing Him as somehow tainted. So God labelled the sin offering "most holy," adding that whatever touched it became holy.

At the very moment He became sin with our sin, He was most holy in God's eyes. He "committed no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth." And because we've touched Him by faith, we've been made holy too. Let that guard how you think of Him, and of yourself.

text: Never judge your standing by your state. Judge your state by your standing.
explanation:
Your state goes up and down: some days you're joyful, some days angry, depressed, tempted. Your standing never changes: in Christ, you are the righteousness of God. You weren't made righteous by your obedience, so your disobedience can't make you unrighteous. "By one Man's obedience many will be made righteous."

The devil wants to define you by your latest failure. Don't deny the sin or excuse it. Look it in the eye and say, "This isn't who I am. I'm not an angry person or a fearful person. I'm the righteousness of God in Christ." Who you are will overcome what you do.

text: Of David's many sons, God chose Bathsheba's to be king. The mouth that denied Jesus preached at Pentecost.
explanation:
"Where sin abounded, grace abounded much more." The word for sin abounding means increase, something you can count. Grace hyperperisseuo: overflowing, and then more piled on top. And grace abounds at the very location where sin increased.

David sinned grievously with Bathsheba. Yet from that same woman came Solomon, whom God chose above all David's other sons. Peter denied Jesus three times with oaths and curses; weeks later, that same mouth preached the first gospel sermon, and three thousand were saved. That's no licence to sin. It's hope: the place of your greatest failure can become the place of your greatest testimony.

text: "Lord, I give You my whole life, including my stutter." He chose the very weakness to display His grace.
explanation:
As a schoolboy, Joseph Prince stammered so badly he could barely string a sentence together. A teacher would make him stand and read aloud just to watch his ears turn red while classmates laughed. When he was saved, he felt almost sorry for the Lord: "You didn't get much. I don't think I can even share the gospel with a friend. But I give You my whole life, plus my stuttering."

He never imagined he'd preach. Yet the very area where he fell short became the place God's grace overflowed. "My strength is made perfect in weakness." Don't hide your weakness from God. Hand it to Him, and watch it become the platform for His glory.

text: Paul was accused of saying "Let us sin that grace may abound." If no one accuses us of that, are we preaching his gospel?
explanation:
"Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? Certainly not! How shall we who died to sin live any longer in it?" Paul raised the question because people were already slandering him: "Let us do evil that good may come." Martyn Lloyd-Jones, the famous Westminster preacher, once observed that if our preaching never draws that accusation, perhaps we aren't preaching grace the way Paul did.

Notice Paul's answer. He doesn't say, "Try hard not to." He says it's impossible to live in sin, because you died to it. A true believer may stumble into sin, but can't make it a home. Grace that's truly understood doesn't produce licence. It produces people who have no desire to go back.
